metadata.title: Sample Tasks from the PISA 2000 Assessment (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This document is a framework/instrument description for PISA 2000 rather than an empirical analysis paper. It explains that PISA 2000 used pencil-and-paper written tasks administered in schools under independently supervised test conditions, with a total assessment time of about seven hours distributed across nine assessment booklets so that each student received a subset of tasks. The report does not provide any student-level analytic dataset, sampling frame, or weight variable names (e.g., TOTWGT, W_FSTUWT) and therefore does not specify how complex survey weights or replicate weights would be applied. For users who later analyze PISA 2000 microdata, the appropriate approach would be to use the official PISA sampling/survey weights and replicate weights supplied with the dataset, and to apply the standard PISA scaling/PV procedures for cognitive literacy scales; however, those details are not operationalized in this instrument-only publication.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This publication does not conduct an empirical student-level analysis predicting outcomes; it documents the conceptual framework, task design, and scoring/scale interpretation for PISA 2000 sample tasks. Because there is no dependent variable modeled from PISA microdata and no reported estimation procedure, plausible values handling and missing-data handling are not part of the study’s methodology. As a result, the PV and missing-data fields are not applicable to the document’s purpose, and missing-data handling is not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report describes PISA 2000 administration and task design rather than an analytic subsample. It states that the first PISA survey was conducted in 2000 in 32 countries (including 28 OECD member countries) with written tasks answered by students in schools under independently supervised test conditions, and that a total of seven hours of assessment tasks were included with different students taking different combinations of tasks. It also notes that each student participated in a written assessment session of two hours and spent about half an hour responding to a background questionnaire, while school principals completed a separate 30-minute questionnaire. No additional inclusion/exclusion criteria for an analytic dataset (e.g., grade restrictions, missing-data exclusions, or task completion filters) are specified in this instrument description.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD publication documents the PISA 2000 assessment instruments and scoring approach for reading, mathematical, and scientific literacy, including the three-dimensional literacy framework (process, content, context) and examples of sample tasks. It explains that PISA 2000 used pencil-and-paper tasks administered in schools, with a total of seven hours of assessment tasks distributed across nine assessment booklets so that each student received a subset of tasks, while still covering the full domain content. The report describes how tasks are classified by the framework dimensions and how responses are scored (including partial credit and double-digit coding for some open-ended items). It also provides guidance for interpreting the resulting proficiency scales (e.g., anchor points and score ranges) and clarifies that the emphasis is on applying knowledge and skills to real-life contexts rather than curriculum mastery alone. No predictive modeling results are reported because the document is an instrument/measurement description rather than an empirical ML study.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a PISA instrument documentation report, not an empirical study estimating relationships between predictors and outcomes. Consequently, there is no student-level analytic model, no ML algorithm evaluation, no reported predictive performance metrics, and no PV/missing-data handling strategy tied to an estimation procedure. The extraction therefore leaves ML and finding tables empty while still capturing the assessment design elements (task structure, scoring, and scale interpretation) that are central to understanding how PISA 2000 measures literacy.
